data.content_ref: inline:The target's defense creates a performative contradiction: it claims scientists 'prefer' better-corroborated theories to 'maximize the growth of knowledge,' yet simultaneously denies that this preference implies any expectation of future success. If corroboration offers no rational basis to expect a theory to survive future tests (predictive reliability), then choosing it over a falsified or less-tested theory is arbitrary with respect to the goal of learning. One cannot coherently argue that Action A is the optimal method for achieving Goal B (knowledge growth) while asserting that Action A provides no more reason to expect Goal B than Action C. Thus, the preference implicitly smuggles in an inductive assumption—that past performance is a relevant guide to future utility—which the target explicitly tries to reject.
